name: Morris Pettaway
languages: The miners' rail-tap signals (knocks on rail or pipe that carry a quarter of a mile underground)
equipment: Heavy coat: a canvas work coat lined with blanket, black with coal dust in the seams
Crowbar, his own, five feet of hexagonal steel he has carried from Alabama to Pittsburgh and back
Double-barrel shotgun, a 12-gauge he keeps in the rafters of his company house and takes squirrel hunting on Sundays, which the guards do not know about
A carbide cap lamp, a canteen of water for it and a tin of carbide
A company brass check, No. 341, for his lamp; and his brother's pay envelope from October 1919, empty, with no number on it
A tool roll: wrenches, a cold chisel, a file, a hammer, wire, tape and spare bits for the cutting machine
A photograph of himself and his brother Ezell in their Sunday suits in a Birmingham studio, 1917
A pay statement from the Ottway company store for the first half of March: earned $41.20, deducted $43.85 for rent, powder, carbide, doctor, smithing and the store, balance due the company $2.65
features: Up Before Dawn (Farm-Raised origin: needs only 6 hours for a long rest; can't be surprised while awake in the last hour before sunrise; advantage on saves against exhaustion from hard work, cold and lost sleep; notices without a check when animals are frightened or behaving wrongly, and the mine mules at Ottway have been very wrong since March)

Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, drops to 1 hit point instead of 0 if not killed outright; ignores his first level of exhaustion; advantage on CON saves against exhaustion, cold and hard labor, and against bad air underground)

Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something, a door, a fallen timber, a stopping, a loaded car off a man; counts as one size larger for carrying and can carry an unconscious adult at full speed)

Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check, he turns the fear into anger: no Dread, but on his next turn he must move toward the source and attack it or break whatever stands between them)

Trade: Longshoreman (Roughneck, 3rd level: one winter on the Mobile docks; advantage on Athletics checks to grapple, shove or hold a door, and a creature he grapples has disadvantage on checks to escape)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: he runs a Jeffrey cutting machine underground and can fix it, a mine motor, a pump or a car; a few minutes with a machine tells him what is wrong with it without a check, including whether someone made it go wrong)

personality.traits: I don't say much, and when I do it's usually a number: inches of roof, tons in a car, days since. I listen to rock. I hum hymns when I work and stop the moment anyone hears me.
personality.ideals: A man ought to be counted. When he's living, by his own check on his own coal. When he's dead, by his own name on a stone.
personality.bonds: My brother Ezell, who is behind the 7 North seal and is on nobody's list. Our mother in Hale County, who asks in every letter when I am bringing him home. Moses Hairston, who loaded beside him and whose check they both worked on.
personality.flaws: I have been patient for eight years and I am done with it. If I have to choose between doing a thing the right way and getting my brother out, I will not choose the right way. I don't trust any white man in this camp, and I know that's not fair to some of them.

appearance: A broad, quiet Black man of thirty-four, a little under six feet, with heavy shoulders, big careful hands with coal tattooed into every old cut, a close-cropped head greying at the temples, and a carbide burn scar on his left cheek. Overalls, work coat, a cap with a lamp bracket, and a way of standing still and listening before he goes into any room.
backstory: Morris Pettaway was raised on a sharecropped cotton farm in Hale County, Alabama, worked the iron-ore mines outside Bessemer at eighteen, and came north to the West Virginia smokeless field in 1917 with his younger brother Ezell, because the coal companies were sending labor agents south with railroad tickets and the pay was twice Alabama's. They worked Ottway No. 3 for two years. Morris ran a cutting machine; Ezell, who was twenty-four and new to coal, loaded as the helper of Moses Hairston, a deacon at Mount Moriah, on Moses's check, which was how a lot of new men started: the coal they loaded together went down on Moses's number and Moses paid him his share. On 14 October 1919 Ezell and Moses were at the face in 7 North when it blew. Morris was in 4 South and ran toward it with the rescue party until the afterdamp turned them back. The company's list of the dead had thirteen names. Ezell's was not on it, because Ezell had no check; when Morris went to the office, a clerk told him that the company had no record of any such man, and that if his brother had been in 7 North the company would have known. Morris left Ottway in 1920 and worked at the Homestead steel works for six years. This February he heard from Rev. Augustus Greer that the company was talking about reopening 7 North this summer, and he came back, and they hired him again, because he is the best cutting-machine man they ever had. He means to be there when that seal comes down, and bring his brother out, and see him buried under his own name in Hale County. He has been on the night shift since March, and twice he has heard, on the 7 North track rail, something knocking the old signals: four, then two.
